questions.q: In the Meridian Health Partners case study, what governance gap from Lesson 2 is identified as the root cause that let `Treatment_Notes__c` go unclassified for three years?
options: Salesforce doesn't allow custom fields on the Contact object
The field was created on the wrong object entirely
No one was ever named the Contact object's data owner, so there was no one with the standing to require review of a new field holding health data before it shipped
The Support rep who created the field lacked a Salesforce license
questions.explain: The case study traces the gap backward to the absence of a named data owner for Contact, which meant no one had the authority to flag the new field for review before it went live.

questions.q: Why does the erasure request in this case study require action beyond deleting the Contact record and `Treatment_Notes__c` field value inside Salesforce?
options: Because GDPR only applies to data stored outside of Salesforce
Because the data has also been syncing nightly to a third-party appointment-reminder tool, and Salesforce deletion doesn't automatically propagate erasure to that downstream system
It doesn't -- deleting the Salesforce record is the entire scope of the request
Because erasure requests cannot legally apply to health data
questions.explain: This is the downstream-propagation problem from Lesson 8: data that left Salesforce via an unmaintained integration still needs to be found and addressed, not just the source record.

questions.q: Once `Treatment_Notes__c` is finally classified in response to the audit finding, what should that classification concretely drive, per this lesson?
options: A mandatory renaming of the field to remove all health-related terminology
Nothing further -- applying the label is the entire task
Automatic deletion of the field within 24 hours
Decisions about whether the field needs Shield Platform Encryption, Field Audit Trail's extended retention for traceability, and inclusion in the next access review
questions.explain: Consistent with Lesson 9's point that classification only has value once it drives downstream decisions, the case study ties the new classification to encryption, audit-retention, and access-review follow-up.

questions.q: Why does this lesson distinguish "fixing the incident" from "fixing the governance gap"?
options: Incidents and governance gaps are entirely unrelated concepts

Resolving this specific patient's request and classifying this specific field handles the immediate problem, but doesn't prevent an identical incident on a different field/object unless the underlying structural gaps (no data owner, no release checkpoint, no integration steward) are also fixed
They are the same action and don't need to be distinguished
Governance gaps can never actually be fixed once they occur
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates the immediate remediation from the structural fix, warning that without the structural fix, a similarly-named `Field_47__c` could become next year's identical incident.

questions.q: What skill does this lesson say the case study is really testing?
options: Memorizing exact Salesforce Shield pricing tiers
Recalling the exact wording of GDPR Article 17 from memory
The ability to write Apex trigger code from scratch
The ability to look at a messy, multi-lesson real situation and correctly assign each piece of the fix to the right role, mechanism, and timeframe (immediate vs. structural)
questions.explain: The lesson states directly that this is a judgment exercise in correctly routing each piece of a real, compounded problem to the right role and timeframe -- exactly what a Technical Architect needs to do with a real client's ungoverned org.
